- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- running-the-suite: Running this repo's test suite — the one command that covers it, reading a run's output from a file instead of re-running it, iterating on the tests an edit touches, and staging a new test file before certifying a run. Use before any node --test.
- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, size the links (how many PRs, what each one's diff is predicted to touch and the automerge policy that prediction becomes) and write the chain to survive a policy park, a red CI or a PR closed unmerged, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. {"number":1773,"title":"Date the three action checks added today so they do not convict the past","body":"`git-pull-on-shallow-clone`, `github-api-via-shell` and `merge-main-into-branch` landed in b1363395 (#1711) at 06:49 UTC today, all `blocking`, none carrying `since`.

An action check is re-judged **over the whole session transcript** at Stop, so a blocking one with no creation date convicts calls made before the check existed in the session's tree. That happened within the hour: a `curl … api.github.com` at ~06:45 ran with nothing to stop it — the guard was genuinely not in that checkout — and became a blocking Stop finding at 06:56 once `main` was synced.

And an action finding has **no clearing move**: a file finding is cleared by editing the file, `skill-loaded-before-editing` by loading the skill, but a past tool call cannot be un-made, so it blocks every Stop for the rest of that session.

`applyGrace` is the corpus's own answer — a rule declaring `since` is advisory for `GRACE_DAYS`, on the stated reasoning that *"absence must mean mature, never newborn"*. The pack already follows this for its other recent blocking rules (`legacy-tolerance-scheduled` 2026-09-03, `hook-judges-never-exit` 2026-09-05); today's three simply missed it.

**`.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/`** — `"since": "2026-09-06"` on those three. They still fire and still say the same thing; they start blocking on the 20th, by which time no session's transcript predates them. `home-seeded-packs-declared` is untouched — it dates from 2026-09-01 and is genuinely mature.

Patched as anchored text, not a re-serialize, so key order and formatting are unchanged (3 insertions, 0 deletions). 59 local-pack tests pass.

Left for its own decision, in the issue: whether a blocking *action* check should ever judge calls from before its `since` at all. Grace expires; the retroactive-transcript problem returns the next time one lands mid-session.

Closes #1772

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Extract lessons from a conversation

Read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions taken in it — and convert its friction into
changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer and less dependent on human steering. Read how the
work went; what the work committed is [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md)'s.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
  A small line-count `offset`/`limit` is not a safe way to `Read` the checked-out file: one JSONL line
  can be a single `tool_use`/`tool_result` running tens of thousands of characters, so even a short
  window can overflow the read cap. Check line lengths first (e.g. `awk '{print length}' <file> |
  sort -n | tail`) or condense the file with a script before attempting a raw read.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

{"number":1787,"title":"Make a blocking action check date itself","body":"Closes #1784

`declared-check-since` — a coded world rule in `basics`, beside its two `declared-check-*` siblings — blocks a `scope: action` declaration at `severity: blocking` that carries no `since`. It judges every `declared-checks.json` in the tree, canon packs and a member's own local packs alike, and it asks the engine's `graceUntil` whether a declared date actually buys grace rather than restating the format, so `"since": "last tuesday"` is the same finding as no `since` at all.

Its first run against the real tree found three live offenders: `grep-context-without-content`, `generated-file-hand-edit` and `wakeup-without-prompt` in `packs/basics/declared-checks.json`. #1773 dated the local pack's three; these three landed undated in the same window (#1711) and were missed. They are dated here to 2026-09-06, the day they landed, so no grace is granted that they had not already spent.

The rule carries its own `since`, so a member holding an undated blocking action check reads the finding for two weeks before it blocks, and the remedy is a one-line edit in their own pack.

### The second half of #1784, not done here

The issue also carries #1772's open question: should a blocking action check judge calls from before its own `since` **at all**? Dating each new check treats the symptom on a 14-day timer; ignoring pre-`since` calls would end the class. That is an engine change to how the Stop-time action judge reads the transcript, and it wants its own decision and its own issue — say the word and I will open it.

### Folders touched

- `packs/basics/worldRules/` — the new `declared-check-since` rule.
- `packs/basics/` — `declared-checks.json` dates the three undated blocking action checks; `README.md` gains the catalog row.
- `vendoring/rehearsal/` — the `local-declared-checks` fixture consumer grows a dated blocking action check, so the rule's accept case is proven on a real converge rather than only in the canon's own tree (the `consumer-safe-change` check's fixture half; the change is additive, so no migration record).

`check_the_work` and `check_the_world` are both 0 blocking; the suite is green but for the pre-existing `engine-pack-lane-shims` shallow-clone guard, which fails identically on `main` in this sandbox.

{"number":1726,"title":"Pack versions are cut on main by automation, never in the pull request","body":"A change under `packs/<id>/` no longer bumps that pack's version, and no check asks it to.

**The bump moves to `main`.** `packs/claudinite-canon-curation/pack-versions.mjs` walks the base branch to each pack's last version bump and asks whether any shipping file under `packs/<id>/` changed since (tests and `VERSIONS.md` excluded, as before). Every such pack takes today's next version, in one commit pushed straight onto `main` with git plumbing — never a force push, replanned from the new tip if `main` moved under it, and stamped `Claudinite-Task:` so the silence gate reads it as machinery.

Two triggers run that one worker:
- `.github/workflows/pack-versions.yml` on every push to `main` (and `workflow_dispatch`), so a version lands minutes after the merge that needs it. A reviewed barrier exception in `.claudinite-settings.json` lets the workflow name the pack's worker.
- the daily `claudinite-canon-curation/pack-version-bump` task, for the merges GitHub turns into no push run — every pull request the queue lands with the Action's own token.

**The checks are gone.** `pack-version-bumped` and `pack-version-claimed-once` are deleted with their tests, README and references rows, the canon-curation "re-bump after a stacked PR lands" rule, and every task/skill sentence telling a run to bump or write a row (growth's `rule-revalidation`, `prose-to-checks-sweep`, canon-curation's `upstream-watch`, basics' `writing-migration-plans`).

**`VERSIONS.md` becomes a derived record.** The weekly `claudinite-canon-curation/pack-version-history` task retraces from git which pull requests landed between one version and the next (squash-merge subjects carry the numbers), writes only the rows a record lacks — hand-written rows stand — and lands them on a self-amending pull request under a `pack-version-history` diff class (`merge-rules.json`) that covers `packs/*/VERSIONS.md` and nothing else. Run against the real history it regenerates all 34 records in about ten seconds and plans no bump today, so the repo is at rest.

**#1689** (two rows claiming `60903.5`): the file on `main` already holds one folded row, and the check that failed on it no longer exists; the automatic bump after this merge re-delivers `claudinite-growth` under a fresh number, which is what the collision had stranded.

**Verification after merge:** the push of this PR itself fires `pack-versions.yml` for the first time and should cut versions for every pack this diff touched (canon-curation, growth, basics, chrome-extension, static-website, claudinite-lifecycle). If that run's push is refused, `main` carries a rule the Action's token cannot satisfy, and the run says so.

Closes #1723

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A schema property** — when the lesson is about a document's *shape*: a field that must be present, a
59	   value from a closed set, a type, a key set nothing may extend. It belongs in the JSON Schema the document
60	   points at with `$schema` (created from the first such rule where the document has none), which an editor
61	   shows while the document is written and the engine's `schema-conformance` check enforces for every such
62	   document at once. Anything a schema can enforce is better handled there: a declared `checkParsedFiles`
63	   assertion over a field, or a coded rule re-reading a document's shape by hand, is a schema check in
64	   disguise. Only what a schema cannot say — a relation between two documents, a value that depends on the
65	   tree — goes on to the rungs below.
66	2. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
67	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. Declare it at the moment its signature
68	   lives: a **world** check over the tree — one pass ("these patterns over these files"), or two when a value
69	   read in one place must agree with, exist in or be absent from another (`extractValueSets` derives the set,
70	   `checkSetValues`/`checkSetPairs`/`requireIdenticalFiles` quantify over it); a **work** check over the
71	   change (`scope: "work"` — the lines it adds or removes, a co-change, an untracked file, the session's
72	   declared comment classes); or an **action** guard on a tool call (`scope: "action"`, `guardToolCalls` —
73	   denied or nudged at PreToolUse, backstopped over the transcript at Stop). Most captured conditions are
74	   one of these, and a lesson about *how an operation is performed* is usually the third. Give it
75	   `severity: 'blocking'` and `since: '<today>'`: the engine holds a check to advisory for its first two
76	   weeks, so a check may land against a tree that still violates it and the backlog it surfaces is somebody
77	   else's next change, not this run's.
78	3. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
79	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
80	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
81	   to read and maintain for nothing. An **unattended** run ships one `advisory`: hand-written logic has
82	   failure modes a declaration cannot have, and nobody reviewed this one.
83	4. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure or a bias rather than a condition —
84	   and name the moment it must load under its `metadata`: `force-load-on-file-edits-paths`,
85	   `force-load-on-tool-calls` (opening a PR, committing, merging, fetching), `force-load-on-prompts-matching`
86	   (an owner's command phrase) or `force-load-on-tool-results-matching` (a symptom in a result). A skill
87	   with no trigger loads on description alone, which is model discretion; a procedure keyed to an act has a
88	   call to name, and rules sharing a trigger belong in one skill so one load carries the whole procedure.
89	5. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
90	
91	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
92	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
93	both rungs — with the `since` grace window — in
94	[`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
95	
96	**Two check shapes are below the bar however cleanly they'd be written**: one that asserts particular code
97	exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time and reds the next legitimate edit), and one
98	derivable from the product's own requirements (that is a requirement — it belongs in the tests).
99	
100	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
101	relocates it. **Prose is rationed, and the ration is small** — a pass adds at most two rules, each one
102	sentence. How a rule is phrased and sized, and where its rationale goes — the brief rule in `RULES.md`, the
103	reaffirmable reason in the pack's `references.md` — is the
104	[writing-pack-prose](skills/writing-pack-prose/SKILL.md) skill's; load it before writing any. The full
105	evidence trail stays in the PR body and the issue.
106	
107	When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
108	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
109	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
110	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
111	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
112	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
113	
114	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all, and it is not this pass's to land either.** A
115	trap from misusing a specific API, class, or library belongs as a comment at that usage site — and a capture
116	run's write surface stops at its own packs, so **drop the candidate** rather than inflate it into a pack
117	rule or collect it into a centralized gotchas list. The comments in a repo's own source belong to the
118	tidy-repo pack's `improve-comments` task, which has its own trigger and its own review surface. Reserve a
119	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
120	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
121	
122	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
123	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
124	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
125	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
126	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
127	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
128	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
129	
130	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
131	
132	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
133	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
134	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
135	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.
136

input.prompt:
You're helping with the "growth-extract" pass on the Claudinite repo, a git repo checked out at /home/user/Claudinite. This pass mines captured agent↔user conversation logs for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, wasted wall-clock waits) that should become durable rules in the repo's own local packs (`.claudinite/local/packs/`).

The repo has an orphan branch `origin/conversation-logs` (already fetched into this local checkout) holding one JSONL file per captured session, named `<ISO-timestamp>--issue-<n>--<session-uuid>.jsonl`. Read one with: `git show origin/conversation-logs:<filename>`.

IMPORTANT: a single JSONL line can be a huge tool_use/tool_result running tens of thousands of characters — do NOT blindly `cat`/`Read` a whole file into your context. First check line lengths, e.g.:
`git show origin/conversation-logs:<filename> | awk '{print length}' | sort -n | tail`
Then read selectively — e.g. extract just the human/assistant text turns (skip huge tool_result blobs), or grep for markers like error/failed/wait/sleep/again/sorry/actually/no I meant/correct/misunderstood, or pull out timestamps to compute wall-clock gaps between consecutive entries. Use small scripts (python3/jq/awk) piped from `git show` rather than loading whole files via the Read tool.

This is the "hindsight" pass: these are the OLDEST captures still on the branch (from 2026-07-19/20, about 7 weeks old — retention hasn't pruned them). Re-read them fresh: a friction signal that looked situational back then may have recurred since (making it worth landing now), or a lesson landed since may have already made it redundant (skip it if so — you can check by grepping the current RULES.md files under packs/*/RULES.md and .claudinite/local/packs/*/RULES.md for whether the topic is already covered).

Files to scan (6 total, all early captures):
2026-07-19T1509Z--issue-349--f5fb31ea-8056-53f9-a9b4-c6733b42b97d.jsonl
2026-07-19T1620Z--issue-359--5ef731cf-00e5-5baf-bb19-0603ac19bee6.jsonl
2026-07-19T2059Z--issue-366--1952b8c3-d77c-5807-b5b4-f184d8b87478.jsonl
2026-07-19T2127Z--issue-364--8667dde0-cb49-5a8a-a903-b46c6c6e6b78.jsonl
2026-07-19T2142Z--issue-368--e618ea16-26f6-5e3c-aa1c-fd108a7ec95e.jsonl
2026-07-20T1358Z--issue-373--9c126afc-d539-5f97-9f6e-59b1ae2c516f.jsonl

Look for: (1) misunderstandings between agent and user (clarifying round-trips, corrections, "no I meant", an AskUserQuestion whose answer was an obvious default); (2) suboptimal agent actions (backtracks, redundant work, re-running a known-failing command, missing an existing convention/helper later corrected in review); (3) measurable wall-time waste (serial ops that could've been parallel, blind sleeps/polling, waiting past when the result was already in hand) — compute real timestamp deltas, never estimate.

Report back (under 500 words): concrete candidates only, each with file/issue number, the friction pattern, evidence (quoted lines or computed timestamps), and whether you already found it covered in current RULES.md (skip those). If nothing clears the bar, say so plainly and briefly — a complete, valid answer.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/extract-from-conversations

# Extract lessons from a conversation

Read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions taken in it — and convert its friction into
changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer and less dependent on human steering. Read how the
work went; what the work committed is [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md)'s.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
  A small line-count `offset`/`limit` is not a safe way to `Read` the checked-out file: one JSONL line
  can be a single `tool_use`/`tool_result` running tens of thousands of characters, so even a short
  window can overflow the read cap. Check line lengths first (e.g. `awk '{print length}' <file> |
  sort -n | tail`) or condense the file with a script before attempting a raw read.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:

	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:

Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A schema property** — when the lesson is about a document's *shape*: a field that must be present, a
59	   value from a closed set, a type, a key set nothing may extend. It belongs in the JSON Schema the document
60	   points at with `$schema` (created from the first such rule where the document has none), which an editor
61	   shows while the document is written and the engine's `schema-conformance` check enforces for every such
62	   document at once. Anything a schema can enforce is better handled there: a declared `checkParsedFiles`
63	   assertion over a field, or a coded rule re-reading a document's shape by hand, is a schema check in
64	   disguise. Only what a schema cannot say — a relation between two documents, a value that depends on the
65	   tree — goes on to the rungs below.
66	2. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
67	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. Declare it at the moment its signature
68	   lives: a **world** check over the tree — one pass ("these patterns over these files"), or two when a value
69	   read in one place must agree with, exist in or be absent from another (`extractValueSets` derives the set,
70	   `checkSetValues`/`checkSetPairs`/`requireIdenticalFiles` quantify over it); a **work** check over the
71	   change (`scope: "work"` — the lines it adds or removes, a co-change, an untracked file, the session's
72	   declared comment classes); or an **action** guard on a tool call (`scope: "action"`, `guardToolCalls` —
73	   denied or nudged at PreToolUse, backstopped over the transcript at Stop). Most captured conditions are
74	   one of these, and a lesson about *how an operation is performed* is usually the third. Give it
75	   `severity: 'blocking'` and `since: '<today>'`: the engine holds a check to advisory for its first two
76	   weeks, so a check may land against a tree that still violates it and the backlog it surfaces is somebody
77	   else's next change, not this run's.
78	3. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
79	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
80	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
81	   to read and maintain for nothing. An **unattended** run ships one `advisory`: hand-written logic has
82	   failure modes a declaration cannot have, and nobody reviewed this one.
83	4. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure or a bias rather than a condition —
84	   and name the moment it must load under its `metadata`: `force-load-on-file-edits-paths`,
85	   `force-load-on-tool-calls` (opening a PR, committing, merging, fetching), `force-load-on-prompts-matching`
86	   (an owner's command phrase) or `force-load-on-tool-results-matching` (a symptom in a result). A skill
87	   with no trigger loads on description alone, which is model discretion; a procedure keyed to an act has a
88	   call to name, and rules sharing a trigger belong in one skill so one load carries the whole procedure.
89	5. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
90	
91	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
92	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
93	both rungs — with the `since` grace window — in
94	[`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
95	
96	**Two check shapes are below the bar however cleanly they'd be written**: one that asserts particular code
97	exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time and reds the next legitimate edit), and one
98	derivable from the product's own requirements (that is a requirement — it belongs in the tests).
99	
100	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
101	relocates it. **Prose is rationed, and the ration is small** — a pass adds at most two rules, each one
102	sentence. How a rule is phrased and sized, and where its rationale goes — the brief rule in `RULES.md`, the
103	reaffirmable reason in the pack's `references.md` — is the
104	[writing-pack-prose](skills/writing-pack-prose/SKILL.md) skill's; load it before writing any. The full
105	evidence trail stays in the PR body and the issue.
106	
107	When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
108	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
109	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
110	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
111	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
112	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
113	
114	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all, and it is not this pass's to land either.** A
115	trap from misusing a specific API, class, or library belongs as a comment at that usage site — and a capture
116	run's write surface stops at its own packs, so **drop the candidate** rather than inflate it into a pack
117	rule or collect it into a centralized gotchas list. The comments in a repo's own source belong to the
118	tidy-repo pack's `improve-comments` task, which has its own trigger and its own review surface. Reserve a
119	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
120	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
121	
122	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
123	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
124	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
125	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
126	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
127	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
128	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
129	
130	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
131	
132	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
133	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
134	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
135	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

{"number":1737,"title":"Rewrite a task declaration's importers when the module is converted","body":"`convertTaskDeclarations` wrote `task.json` and deleted `task.mjs`, but left every sibling that imported the module with a dangling specifier. The task's worker then fails to load — `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` — the item parks `task:status:needs-human-failure`, and because `failure` is the one **blocking** park kind the lane stops being scheduled entirely. A `failure` park is superseded only by a later clean run of the same task, which the park itself prevents, so the lane cannot recover on its own.

This was found live: missingbulb/Shepherd#449 froze `shepherd/fleet-issues-snapshot` (a **daily** task) on 2026-09-04, the day after the migration landed, and it has produced nothing since.

The converter now rewrites the import in place — preserving quote style, adding the JSON import attribute the runtime requires — in both branches that remove the module, and the report line names the files it touched.

```js
import task from './task.mjs';
// becomes
import task from './task.json' with { type: 'json' };
```

## Verification

The new test fails against the previous converter and passes now. `engine-tests/task-declarations-to-json.test.mjs` + the migrations suite: 57/57 green. `check_the_world.mjs`: 0 blocking.

No `ENGINE_VERSION` bump — `engine-release-record` requires a canary rehearsal run behind any bump, which this change does not carry; it ships on the next engine release.

This fixes the migration going forward. It does **not** repair members already converted — their dangling import is committed. Shepherd's is fixed in that repo separately.

## Folders touched

```
engine/migrations/   convertTaskDeclarations now rewrites the task folder's
                     sibling .mjs importers when it deletes the module
engine-tests/        a case covering an importing worker and test, which
                     fails against the old converter
```

{"number":1707,"title":"A task declares what its run does to pull requests, and the executor resolves the target once","body":"Closes #1695

## The problem

Which pull request a task's run works on was decided in three places, none of them the task's declaration: the update worker disposed of its own incumbent, the generated-file lane reused an open PR by branch prefix, and an agent session picked its own branch with nothing telling it whether one already existed. A task could not say "append to my open PR" at all.

## What changes

**`expected_outcome` becomes four words** that carry the write ceiling and the target policy in one axis: `no_code_changes`, `fresh_pr`, `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr`, `supersede_existing_pr`. The retired `none`/`pr` normalize at the door beside `open-pr`/`merged-pr`, both declaration checks advise the rename, and the retirement rides #1642 with the contract's other tolerances.

**The executor resolves the target once** (`queue/target.mjs`), after the precondition's go and before code-work, and hands it to both phases: code-work as `CLAUDINITE_TARGET_MODE` / `CLAUDINITE_TARGET_BRANCH` / `CLAUDINITE_TARGET_PR`, the agent as `Target-branch:` / `Target-pr:` / `Supersedes:` fields stamped at the hand-off. A task's open pull requests are recognised by the branch prefix the executor mints (`claudinite/<pack>/<task>/`) or by the `Claudinite-Task:` trailer on the head commit. An amend reads the newest incumbent's mergeability and falls back to a fresh branch on a conflict or an unreadable answer. A supersede judges the newest incumbent by the runs on its head: a green, unlanded one on an auto-merge repo is landed and the occurrence ends there; otherwise the incumbents close once the run's own pull request exists, performed by the executor after code-work delivered one and by the session's converge (`--pr`) when the agent did. A run that delivers nothing leaves them where they were.

**The lanes take the target as given.** `deliverGenerated` accepts `branch`/`pr`; the update worker pushes to the branch it is handed. Each keeps its own discovery only under an executor that predates the hand-off, marked `@legacy-tolerance … retire:#1698`.

**What each canon task declares.** `none` tasks declare `no_code_changes`. `update` declares `supersede_existing_pr` (what its disposal already did, moved into the executor) and `usage-fold` `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` (what its prefix reuse already did). By owner decision, nine more change behaviour: prose-to-checks-sweep, growth-extract, wiki-growth, improve-comments, ci-performance, growth-discover-packs and growth-promote amend their open pull request; rule-revalidation and growth-dedup supersede theirs. Their `task.md` files now deliver on the branch and pull request the item names instead of searching for a standing pull request or minting a branch themselves. Three consequences of one branch per run: wiki-growth's `no-open-pr-touching:product-wiki/` precondition retires (the amend is what that gate existed to prevent), a discovery run authors one pack per run rather than one per gap, and a promote run names a technology with no home on its tracker rather than minting the stub in a second pull request. Every other `pr` task declares `fresh_pr`, unchanged in behaviour.

Design: tasks-dispatch DESIGN §6 step 4b and decision §15.32; the sim models no pull request content, so the coverage map points at `queue/target.test.mjs` and the executor loop's tests.

## Verification

- Every new test was written red first: contract, declaration checks, work-item fields, converge ops, code-work env, the target planner and its I/O shell, the executor loop, the lanes, and the nine tasks' declarations and worker docs.
- Full suite over `git ls-files '*.test.mjs'`: 3265 tests, 0 failures.
- `check_the_work --changed --base origin/main`: no findings. `check_the_world`: 0 blocking; the one advisory on a touched file (`file-placement` on the update worker's import) is on a line this branch did not change.
- Production verification (a member's next `update` superseding its open PR; the canon's next `usage-fold` amending its own) is filed by `verify-in-production` after this merges, per basics.

{"number":1756,"title":"Judge a beating agent on its progress, not its punctuality","body":"**Stacked on [#1753](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1753)** — it needs that branch's `agentBeatComment`, so it bases there rather than on `main`. Merging #1753 first re-targets this one automatically.

#1753 gives the agent phase a beat, and creates the hazard this closes: a beat resets the issue clock by existing, so the clock alone makes every beating session **immortal** — including one that wedged an hour in. The signal degrades from "work is happening" to "a process is alive", which is the failure the leash exists to catch.

The beat already carries what separates them: its note is the progress (`9/15 groups triaged`), so a run of beats all saying the same thing is a wedged run, however punctual.

**`packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/`** — `lastProgressAt` answers when the beat note last *changed* (the oldest beat of the trailing run sharing the newest one's note), reading the note back off the rendered comment body since that is the only copy. Rule B (`deadAgentItems`) takes a `progressAt` reader the way `staleReadyItems` takes `periodFor` — injected, so the rule stays pure and the sweep keeps the I/O — and runs its leash from progress when the item has beats, from the issue clock when it has none. `deadAgentComment` says which of the two it was, so a reader knows whether to look for a dead session or a stuck one.

**`packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/task-janitor/`** — the sweep resolves progress only for items actually holding an agent (usually none or one), and hands the rule a finished lookup.

**Rollout is inert until sessions beat.** An item with no beats answers `null` and is judged exactly as today — which is every item on the fleet right now, since nothing beats until #1753's `executor.md` reaches members. No behaviour change lands ahead of the writer.

See-it-fail, three mutations, each biting only its own guard:

| mutation | red |
|---|---|
| rule B back on the issue clock | both leash cases (the stale-clock/live-work and live-clock/dead-work pair) |
| progress = newest beat, not last change | the `lastProgressAt` case |
| no-beats answers a time instead of `null` | the `lastProgressAt` case |

661 tests pass across `claudinite-tasks`; `check_the_world` 0 blocking. The one new advisory is a fifth `file-placement` reach from `queue-sweep.mjs` into `queue/`, identical to the four already there — that file is the I/O shell over `queue/`, the deliberate cross-cutting concern the check's own fix text says to leave.

Closes #1752

{"number":1622,"title":"Retire the precondition() function form — one gate mechanism","body":"Closes #1617

Phase 1f — the removal. **Stacked on #1619**, so this PR's diff is the removal alone; review that one first.

> ⚠️ **Do not merge until the five member PRs have landed.** They are listed below. An invalid declaration is skipped by `discover.mjs:81` with a recorded error rather than failing the mount, so merging this first would stop each member's local task running with nothing red to say so.

## What this reverses

`task-contract.mjs` carried this, and I reported it back as settled fact earlier in the session:

> *"the `precondition` function stays accepted forever, for a member's own local task files, which nothing converges."*

That sentence and every other statement of it is gone. `preconditions` is the only gate a task declares.

## Why removal rather than tolerance

Two forms meant every reader, every check and the evaluator itself had to ask which one was the gate. A task-local term does everything the function did while staying **pure over its inputs** and testable at a chosen instant — which #1619 completes by handing a term the instant its verdict is for, the one thing the function could do that a term could not.

Both retired spellings are rejected **by name** in the contract and the declaration-shape check, so a declaration carrying one is told what replaced it rather than reading as a task that simply forgot its gate.

`taskSignalNames` now has nothing to reconcile: the union has one source, the terms the expression names.

## One deliberate behaviour change

A term that throws returns `{ error }` and the item **parks open** in the failure lane. The function form turned a throw at pick into a *decline* — quietly closing the occurrence on a gate that never answered, after which the next anchor walked into the same throw. A throw is not a verdict. `executor-loop.test.mjs` asserts the new outcome and says why.

## Ordering — the members went first

All six member-local tasks were converted before this, and re-read at HEAD: zero remaining across all 16 adopted members.

- missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator#1142 — `generic-extractor-improvements`, `create-extractor`
- missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite#411 — `site-stats`
- missingbulb/EdFringeNow#586 — `refresh-shows`, `refresh-tickets`
- missingbulb/Shepherd#424 — `fleet-issues-snapshot`

## Surface

Engine: `task-contract.mjs` (both branches + `taskSignalNames`), `queue/executor.mjs`, `queue/scheduler-run.mjs`, `worldRules/task-declaration-shape.mjs`, `claudinite-dashboard/model.mjs`. Prose: `writing-tasks/SKILL.md`, `docs/task-preconditions/DESIGN.md`. The two older DESIGN docs that name the field are historical records of their own migrations and are deliberately left — rewriting them would falsify what they record.

## Assurance

`legacy-precondition-retired.test.mjs` was written first and watched fail (3/6 initially red on the surface the removal changes), then made green. The existing corpus pinned the old form in ~10 files; those fixtures were migrated, with the `test(` count held at 183 across the touched files before and after, per this repo's own rule about bulk rewrites.

Full suite **2983/2983**; `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking.

**Version note:** this bumps `claudinite-growth` to 60902.2, the same number #1612 takes. Whichever lands second needs a re-bump — flagging rather than guessing which order you want.

{"number":1793,"title":"Say the hold's unreadable variable once, and keep verifications inside this repo","body":"Two owner reports, one branch.

## 1. The hold's live read repeated its refusal at every boundary

```
! could not read CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL live (403) — using the value this run started with. …
```

The between-items read (`queue/suspend.mjs`, DESIGN §15.30) asks
`GET /repos/{repo}/actions/variables/…` at each pick. That endpoint is scoped to a token's
variables access, which the workflow `permissions:` block has no key for — DESIGN §15.24 already
said so — so on the Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` the read is refused at every boundary of every drain,
permanently. The line reported the same standing fact once per item, and spent an API call each
time to re-learn it.

`readSuspendedNow` becomes `liveSuspendReader`, a per-run reader: an access refusal (401/403) is a

| Automatically delete head branches | a PR GitHub auto-merges is merged outside `land-pr.mjs`, which is what deletes the branch on the paths it merges itself |

The steps are gated on the repo declaring `claudinite-tasks`: a repo running no scheduled work has no Action-authored pull request for any of the three to affect, and a checklist of no-ops teaches the reader to skim.

Test written first and watched fail on the current block, then green: the hand-over block names all three for a default adoption, and none of them for a `basics`-only repo. Full suite 3302/3302; `check_the_world` 0 blocking.
