{"number":1616,"title":"Dashboard redesign: the fleet ledger, the repo page and the Work board","body":"The whole redesign (#1602), all five phases. Phases 1–2 are the **data**; 3–5 are the **pages** drawn from it.

Phase 1 goes first because its counters accumulate from the day they ship: every page built on them renders a named gap until a member's fold carries them, so the pages cannot lead.

## Phase 1 — the usage fold's new counters (#1603)

Each field follows the file's own rules: a tuple against the `fields` header, **no key where the source could not answer**, a week row grown from the first day that carried it.

| Field | What it carries |
|---|---|
| `tokensByModel` | the same spend split per model, the four counters kept apart so a day is priceable per counter |
| `humanSeconds` / `agentSeconds` | how the sessions' wall clock divided — each turn billed the gap that produced it |
| `prs` | each merged PR's `leadHours`, `issueLeadHours`, `sessionToMergeHours`, past a new `prsFoldedThrough` watermark |
| `taskCost` | `sessions`/`tokensIn`/`tokensOut`/`userMessages` per task |
| `parks` | how often each task needed a human, by kind |
| `ruleTokensByPack` | where a session's rule-token weight came from |

Plus the worker **deepens its shallow checkout** over the day window, so the line counts stop being unknown for every day but today.

Three decisions worth reading: `prs` carries **durations, never percentiles** (a week's p50 is not derivable from its days'); the human-second **cap is declared in the file's own `caps` header**, so the floor is never guessed; and **parks are read from label events**, since an item's final labels say only where it ended.

## Phase 2 — the page-side reads (#1604)

Every figure is a reduction over a response the page already fetches — **the viewer makes no new request**. Merged PRs kept in the projection with `merged_at` and `closesIssue` parsed before the body is dropped; `pricing.mjs` keeping *a number*, *unpriced* and *a priced sum beside an unpriced remainder* strictly apart; the scheduler heartbeat topped up from the fold's hour tier as a floor, so a scheduler older than one page of runs stops reading as one that never ran.

## Phase 3 — the fleet page's top block (#1605)

One ruled sheet, a stub column naming five bands, **no cards**, figures in mono on fixed tracks, and exactly one warm object — the Start-here slip. It replaced the benefits tiles, the glance tiles and two of the four activity charts; each fact moved to where it is acted on.

`fleet-ledger.mjs` **decides** — the window, the three unknown states, each figure's own *bad when*, so a figure with no number carries the sentence saying why and a quotient inherits both its inputs' gaps. `sheet.mjs` **renders** — one function per mark, the heartbeat, wake strip, pulse and sparklines all the same square at four scales.

**The wake strip states an absence.** A task's anchor lives in its own declaration, and a fleet read carries task *paths*, not contents; fetching them is one request per task per member. An empty strip reads as *nothing wakes* — the serious verdict — so the cell says it was not read.

## Phase 4 — the repo page's block and the Work board (#1606)

The block is the fleet's ledger one member deep, with a machine that asks a different question one level down: its heartbeat is one square per **hour**, beside CI on main, whose failing state is the one critical on the block. `repo-ledger.mjs` adds the three questions only a repo can ask — the queue's own outcome **words** (an obsolete share; `none` above zero meaning items closed without converging at all), this repo's corpus weight against the fleet mean, and the per-task expand with tokens-per-close beside the model each task runs on.

**The board.** The lane is the flow: a row is a connected component of the `Blocked-by` / `Ends-when` / `Closes` graph — never one task (that hides the chain: an approval park is nothing without the PR it holds) and never one kind (that puts the two ends of one edge in different rows, and the edge *is* the finding).

Three placements are its whole argument: a stamped `Not-before` **is** the schedule; a relative one is **flagged rather than guessed**, because it is a date the machine will treat as absent; and a plain issue nobody is scheduled to close gives its downstream item **no time at all** — drawn as a broken lane, and said in words.

The Scheduled group is a task × day grid where a failure park lands on its **own task's row**, so a hatched cell followed by filled ones is the record disagreeing with the roster's held-lane claim, read left to right on one line.

## Phase 5 — the explore panels (#1607)

One per status, because the reader's next move differs by status, and every one ends in a single imperative. Every field names its source; a field the page cannot read says **not read** rather than being omitted — a PR's size, the checks on its head sha, a `Refs` edge, each of which costs a request per mark. The converge command they print is spelled as `converge-item.mjs`'s own usage block spells it.

## What each folder changed

```
packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/usage-fold/
  the counters: vocabularies and the caps/prsFoldedThrough header in
  usage-format.mjs, extraction and folding in fold-usage.mjs, the parks read in
  read-queue.mjs, a new read-prs.mjs with its pure derivations in pr-fields.mjs,
  and the history deepen in worker.mjs

packs/claudinite-tasks/shared-code/
  a new pull-requests.mjs publishing those derivations — from the pure module,
  since the consumer is a page that runs in a browser

packs/claudinite-dashboard/
  new: pricing.mjs, fleet-ledger.mjs, sheet.mjs, repo-ledger.mjs, board.mjs,
  board-view.mjs, explore.mjs.  cache.mjs and github.mjs keep merged PRs;
  fleet.mjs tops the heartbeat up from the fold; fleet-growth.mjs gains the
  fleet mean; model.mjs gains wakeStrip; view-fleet.mjs and view-repo.mjs
  render the sheets and the board and drop what moved; index.html carries the
  identity's palette and the board's marks; config.mjs and build-site.mjs
  carry `rates`

engine/pack_loader/
  session-summary.mjs prints a per-pack split of the rule-token weight

packs/claudinite-dashboard/docs/
  five corrections the implementation found in the spec
```

**The sign-in surface is untouched.** `auth.mjs`, `oauth-exchange.mjs`, `deployment-config.mjs` and the deploy task carry no change, and index.html's sign-in markup is byte-identical to `main`'s — the only new config key, `rates`, travels the declaration path beside `canonRepo`, not the repository-variable path the sign-in pair uses. The `data-info` disclosure pairs match `main` exactly apart from `repo-tiles-2`, which went with the tiles it explained.

## Spec corrections

- **`fields.parks`** is the imported `PARK_KINDS`, not a re-spelled list whose order contradicted the file's own rule.
- **The per-pack rule-token facet** loses its thousands separators: the facets are comma-joined, so a comma must stay the segment's terminator.
- **`merged_at`** rides each PR's own stub on the issues endpoint; **`closesIssue`** is parsed by the fold's published rule rather than a second one.
- **`Merge:`** is the field the queue writes and `parseWorkItemBody` reads — not `Automerge:` — so that is what the panel names.
- **`Refs #n` is not read**: the PR projection drops the body once the closing issue is out of it, so that edge would cost a request per PR.

## Verification

Both pages were **rendered against fixtures built from this repo's own data** — its usage fold, and for the repo page its 60 open issues, 24 open PRs and 17 task declarations — through a harness driving the actual page, in light and dark.

| Exit condition | Target | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| fleet: members grid marker | above 900 px @ 1280 | **683 px** |
| repo: Work board begins | above 900 px @ 1280 | **652 px** |
| repo: top block | ≤ 450 px | **486 px** — the two *not recorded* sentences are wrapped lines where a figure is one; the budget bends before the gap goes unstated |
| every unavailable figure | a named gap | *not recorded — this fold predates humanSeconds*, *no merged PR named a closing issue*, *not read — the anchors are in declarations this page does not fetch* |

The board found a real one on this repo while being verified: **#1609's lane is broken — nobody is scheduled to close #1606** — drawn dashed in the critical hue with the finding in words and the panel's imperative under it.

**Rebased onto `main` at f1a223c.** The only conflict was the `claudinite-tasks` version: `main` claimed `60902.4` while this branch was open, so its two rows moved up to `60902.5` and `60902.6` — a version number is claimed once. Both pages re-rendered afterwards to the same measurements above.

Full suite green on the rebased tree: **3,088 tests, 0 failures**. `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` at 0 blocking, with six new advisories, all `file-placement` on cross-pack `shared-code` reaches — the same standing every other dashboard module importing it already has.

Closes #1603

{"number":1786,"title":"Janitor rule I: close a failure park nobody has answered in three weeks","body":"Closes #1785

## The gap

A `failure` park HOLDS ITS TASK'S LANE — `planSchedulerRun` keeps a blocking park in the standing
family, so while one is open no further occurrence of that task is ever filed. That is deliberate,
and `writing-tasks` says so: a queue of items that will break the same way helps nobody, and the
silence is the signal.

What was never bounded is how long the silence lasts. Rule E (the superseded park) is the only
thing that would end such a park, and its answer is "a later clean run of this task converged" —
which the lane hold makes impossible. So a standing item that parks `failure` and is never read by
a person sits forever, and its task is dead with it.

Every other kind terminates: `action` does not hold the lane, so later runs happen and rule E
fires; `approval` ends when its pull request resolves (rule G); `decision` is a choice a person
owes. `failure` alone had nothing.

Seen in missingbulb/TLDR#275 — parked by the agent leash (`needs-human`, `origin:schedule`),
untouched for over three weeks.

## The fix

Rule I, the abandoned failure park. A standing occurrence wearing a `failure` park and untouched
for **10 days** closes `task:status:rejected` (clearing the park, legacy bare `needs-human`
included) and closes the issue `not_planned` — which also releases the lane, so the next scheduled
run either succeeds or re-parks against a current trace rather than a stale one.

Guards, all of them narrowing:

- **standing items only**, structurally (`isStandingItem` against the declaration at HEAD) — a
  qualified item, a `manual` task's item and an adopted ad-hoc issue are each somebody's own work,
  and no clock answers those. A task absent from HEAD is rule F's, not this one's.
- **`failure` only** — the other three kinds are a person's inbox rather than a fault report.
- an empty task set reads as *unknown*, never "everything retired", as everywhere else the janitor
  reads HEAD.
- a fresh read immediately before acting, like the stateless repair and rule H: a person part-way
  through diagnosing the fault may have touched the item since the sweep's snapshot, and that touch
  is exactly the answer the bound was waiting for.

Rules E, F and G still win where they also apply — naming the run that answered a park, or the
pull request that ended it, says more than the clock does.

### Owner decisions on this rule

- **Ten days, not three weeks** — the bound a park nobody has read has earned.
- **Every failure park, not only the agent leash's** — the rule was offered narrowed to parks whose
  record is the leash's own escalation, with a comment-only posture for the rest; the owner took
  the wide rule. The cost accepted with it: a genuinely reproducible worker bug re-parks on a
  ten-day cycle and its age does not accumulate on one issue.

## Folders touched

- `packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/` — `janitor-rules.mjs` gains rule I: `ABANDONED_PARK_MS`,
  `abandonedParkItems`, `abandonedParkComment`, and `frequencyForTasks` (the HEAD-declaration
  lookup its standing test needs, alongside the existing `periodForTasks`).
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/task-janitor/` — the sweep runs the rule after E/F/G and before H,
  retires through the same `retire` helper the other closing rules use, and counts it in the health
  line.
- `packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/` — the lane-hold paragraph now says the hold is
  bounded, since that is the contract a task author reads.

## Verification

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 3253 pass, 0 fail. `check_the_world`: 0 blocking.

Every guard was watched biting. The five negative tests can't be written red — the pre-change code
also yields nothing — so each was proven by weakening the guard it covers and restoring with
`git checkout --`:

| mutation | test that went red |
| --- | --- |
| bound → `>= 0` | inside-the-bound park; touched-since-the-read park |
| kind guard → any park | only the failure park is abandoned |
| standing guard dropped | only a standing occurrence; unreadable task set claims nothing |
| fresh re-read dropped | a park touched between the read and the write |
| E/F/G precedence guard dropped | a superseded park is closed as superseded |

No manual step: the nightly converge carries the pack to members, and the daily janitor closes what
is standing.

{"number":1798,"title":"Check that the executor workflow passes every declared secret","body":"A secret reaches a task only if `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml` names it statically. The wiring converge stamps one env line per declared secret — but `.github/workflows/` is the one directory a converge may not push to, so that file is scaffolded once at adoption and never regenerated. Every task and every invocation endpoint added afterwards declares a secret the job does not carry, and nothing says so until a run reaches the endpoint call.

NoRFinder is that case today: an endpoint declaring `tokenSecret: CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` against an executor whose secrets list is empty, two queue items parked `needs-human-action` (missingbulb/NoRFinder#31 is the member-side fix).

`executor-workflow-secrets` recomputes the expectation from the same two sources the converge reads and reports every name the workflow does not pass. Extra names are not a finding — a member that dropped a task keeps a harmless line.

Advisory, for `conformance-workflow`'s reason: the remedy is a human-merged PR to `.github/workflows/`, the one fix a member's own machinery cannot make, so blocking would turn such a member red with no move of its own to clear it.

Checks run: the new test file (6 tests), the whole suite (one pre-existing failure, `engine-pack-lane-shims`, which fails loudly because this checkout is shallow), and `check_the_world` — 0 blocking, and the same 103 advisory as before the change. Seen to fire: dropping `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` from this repo's own executor produces the finding, anchored at the marker line.

Closes #1796

{"number":1734,"title":"Remove tests that only assert a declared value is set; widen the writing-tests rule","body":"Closes #1727

## Methodology

`writing-tests`' rule "Never pin a declaration to itself" becomes **"Never test that a value is set"**: it now covers any declared value (an exported constant, a default object, a settings entry, a workflow line, a frontmatter key), names the looser coats of the same test ("it exists", "it has the right shape", "it is one of these"), and says what to write instead — a test of the behaviour the value drives, run through the real code; where nothing reads the value there is nothing to test. `basics` bumps to 60905.2.

## Cleanup

Every test file was surveyed. About 130 cases pinned a declaration to itself — `task.json` and `pack.mjs` fields, exported constants, directory listings, regexes over `task.md`/`SKILL.md`/README prose or over source text. Three kinds of change:

- **Deleted** the cases whose value drives nothing testable, or whose behaviour a sibling case already exercised. Three files ended with nothing left and are removed: `engine-tests/setup-realignment-parity.test.mjs`, `packs/basics/test/writing-migration-plans.test.mjs`, `packs/claudinite-tasks/test/queue/instructions.test.mjs`.
- **Trimmed** single pin lines out of otherwise behavioural cases (`assert.equal(ROT_DAYS, 14)`, `rule.severity === 'advisory'`, `deepEqual(preconditions, ['none'])` beside an `evaluatePrecondition` drive).
- **Rewrote** ~15 cases so the declared value is fed to the real code: the pack-renames migration applied over a fake mount; `manual` declarations driven through the queue's anchor arithmetic and `planSchedulerRun`; the skill templates in `basics` parsed by the queue's real `parseRequestFields`/`parseVerificationSpec`; workflow-failure labels produced by `reportWorkflowFailure` and decoded back with `originOf`/`statusOf`; the suspend hold proven by running each entry point under it; the sheepdog `code_work` argv run through the real `parseParams`. Each rewritten assertion was flipped once, seen red, and restored.

Test-call count across modified files: 955 → 844, plus the three deleted files. Full suite: `# tests 3165 / # pass 3165 / # fail 0`; `check_the_work` clean.

## Left for follow-up (not in this PR)

Several deleted cases were guarding a convention rather than a behaviour and belong on the check ladder, not in a test: frozen seed workflow stubs carrying no `run:`/`schedule:`/`vars.`; no `toJSON(secrets)` in any workflow stub; the sheepdog pack naming no concrete pack id (a `config.barriers` entry); task workers importing their sibling sweep rather than re-implementing it. Listed on #1727.

Also observed: the `pretooluse` skill gate blocked `Edit`/`Write` from subagents even after the skill was loaded, because it reads the parent session's transcript, where a subagent's tool calls never appear.

{"number":1740,"title":"Group the tidy sweeps' fan-out, and keep the run bound covering it","body":"`tidy-issues` said "for each issue in scope, run the single-issue-triage skill", and a worker reading that dispatches one subagent per issue. Each child re-reads the skill and re-derives what `main` holds to return a verdict that is usually `left` or `unchanged` — the fan-out costs more than everything it decides. It also spends the worker's whole run bound, so the worker returns too late for the executor's step-4 converge: the dispatch issue is never commented, closed or labelled, and sits `agent-running` until the janitor parks it hours later as a failure the run never had.

**`packs/tidy-repo/tasks/`** — both GitHub-object workers now work their scope in their own context and fan out only **by group, never by item**: a handful of groups whose members share what the verification has to read, one subagent each, returning one line per item. `tidy-prs` carries the same rule as the structurally identical surface. Both state that the tracker write and the executor's converge come out of the same bound the fan-out spends, so a partial pass that converges beats a full one that returns late.

**`packs/claudinite-tasks/`** — the executor now tells the subagent plainly that a fan-out inside it does not extend the bound it was handed, and names what a late return costs.

**`packs/claudinite-growth/skills/unattended-agents/`** — the portable lesson: pick a fan-out's unit by what the children would share, and leave the parent budget to converge.

Prose only; `check_the_world` goes 96 → 95 advisories (the new text initially tripped `task-phase-discipline` and was reworded). The three suite failures on this branch are pre-existing and environmental — two `pack-versions` fixtures asserting yesterday's date, and the `engine-pack-lane-shims` shallow-clone guard.

Closes #1739

import subprocess, json, sys, re
from collections import Counter

files = sys.argv[1:]

def get(f):
    r = subprocess.run(["git","show",f"origin/conversation-logs:{f}"], cwd="/home/user/Claudinite", capture_output=True, text=True)
    return r.stdout

for f in files:
    content = get(f)
    lines = content.splitlines()
    is_err_count = 0
    bash_cmds = []
    err_lines = []
    tool_counter = Counter()
    for i, line in enumerate(lines):
        if not line.strip(): continue
        try:
            obj = json.loads(line)
        except Exception:
            continue
        msg = obj.get("message", {})
        if not isinstance(msg, dict): continue
        cl = msg.get("content")
        if not isinstance(cl, list): continue
        for c in cl:
            if not isinstance(c, dict): continue
            t = c.get("type")
            if t == "tool_use":
                tool_counter[c.get("name")] += 1
                if c.get("name") == "Bash":
                    bash_cmds.append((i, str(c.get("input",{}).get("command",""))[:120]))
            if t == "tool_result" and c.get("is_error"):
                is_err_count += 1
                cc = c.get("content")
                s = cc if isinstance(cc,str) else json.dumps(cc)
                err_lines.append((i, str(s)[:200]))
    print(f"=== {f} === is_error_count={is_err_count} bash_calls={tool_counter.get('Bash',0)} tools={dict(tool_counter)}")
    for i,s in err_lines[:10]:
        print(f"   ERR L{i}: {s}")
    print()

{"number":1619,"title":"preconditions: hand a term the instant its verdict is for","body":"Phase 1a of #1617 — retiring the legacy `precondition()` function form.

## Why this is first

A term's `holds` received `{ arg, config, item, windowDays }` and **no clock**. That is fine for every term the canon has today, all of which read a window of signals. It is fatal for one of the six member-local tasks still on the function form: `edfringe/refresh-tickets` gates purely on the instant — August, Edinburgh time — so it has nothing in the signal bundle to read.

Without this, that conversion has nowhere to go, and the migration cannot finish. Having the term reach for the process clock itself is not the alternative: it would be untestable at a chosen moment and impure, in the one module whose header promises to be neither.

## The change

`evaluatePreconditions` takes `now` and passes it into `holds`. Both callers already hold the instant they are deciding for — `scheduler-run.mjs` its anchor, `executor.mjs` the `at` its own signals were collected for — so the value is threaded, never read. That also means a clock-reading term and a windowed one cannot disagree about when "now" is.

Additive: every existing term ignores the new key, and the full suite is unchanged at 2977 passing.

## Assurance

The tests were written first and watched fail (2/2), using a term whose subject is the instant. They assert both the policy function and the `evaluatePrecondition` seam production actually goes through — a precondition that passes a direct-call test and throws on every real run is the failure that seam exists to prevent, per its own header.

Full suite 2977/2977; `check_the_work` clean.

{"number":1612,"title":"The weekly sweeps append to their standing PR instead of standing down","body":"Closes #1611

## The change

Three weekly tasks each declined a round while its predecessor sat unreviewed — `prose-to-checks-sweep`, `rule-revalidation` (via a guard added earlier in this PR) and `improve-comments` (which has had one all along).

That trades a smaller review for a slower one. The backlog does not shrink while the round is skipped; the reviewer still has to read the same work, just later and in more pieces.

A round now **runs and pushes onto the open PR's branch**, found by the subject its worker doc pins. One review covers several weeks of conversions, corrections or comment work — a bigger diff, but more of it per arrival of attention.

| task | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `prose-to-checks-sweep` | `['repo-active', 'no-open-pr-titled:…']` | `['repo-active']` |
| `rule-revalidation` | `['repo-active', 'no-open-pr-titled:…']` | `['repo-active']` |
| `improve-comments` | `[…, 'no-open-pr-titled:Claudinite tidy: improve comments']` | the first two conditions only |

## The pinned subject survives, with a better job

It was how the gate recognised a pending round. It is now how a round **finds the PR to join**. Each worker doc says the same thing: search the repo's *open* PRs for that exact title, push onto its branch if one exists, open one if not.

That also means no state is carried between runs. A merged or closed round is not open, so the next run starts a fresh PR by itself — nothing has to remember which round is current.

`rule-revalidation` gets one extra instruction: its PR body is **appended to, never replaced**. A reviewer cannot re-derive a probe result from the diff, so an earlier round's evidence must not be overwritten by a later round's.

## What still must not change

Neither growth task may be narrowed to a movement gate. Both work a **standing backlog**, so gating on prose or claims changing would halt the sweep half-worked the week its subject stopped moving. That constraint is now the only comment at either declaration.

## Accepted trade-off

An unreviewed PR grows every week with no ceiling. That is deliberate: its size is the signal it is overdue, and capping it would re-introduce exactly the stacking this removes.

## Assurance

The tests that asserted the guard now assert its absence and that a pending round still runs, plus that each worker doc pins its delivery subject and tells the round to append. `improve-comments`' three-way title pin becomes a two-way one binding the scope check's commit-subject marker to the worker doc.

Full suite 2979/2979; `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking.

adoption flow), never a conformance finding —
    [packs/README.md](../../packs/README.md#adoption-interview-questions). A stored answer whose
    question the pack no longer declares is an *advisory* `config` finding.
  - **rules** / **accept** — severity overrides and acceptances **motivated by declaring this
    pack**; they may name *any* rule (declaring pack A can require an exemption to pack B's
    check), and the entry is their provenance — the file says which declaration required which
    exception. Same shapes as the top-level keys; entry-sourced acceptances surface with the
    pack named. Two sources disagreeing on a rule's severity is a settings error, never a
    silent last-writer-wins.
  - **via** — written by the engine (never by hand) when a dependency is materialized:
    the declared packs that directly require this one, kept accurate by the update
    backfill (an empty recomputed `via` marks an orphan the project can drop).
- **rules** — per-rule severity override: `"off"` / `"advisory"` / `"blocking"`. The top-level
  key holds project-wide overrides and those for skill-owned checks (which run
  pack-independently, so no pack entry can carry them).
- **accept** — reviewed, reasoned exemptions. `path` matches exactly, or a whole subtree when it
  ends with `/`; omit it to accept the rule everywhere. The `reason` is mandatory — a reasonless
  acceptance is itself a blocking finding. The top-level key holds project-origin exemptions (the

{"number":1733,"title":"Scheduling is the task's own precondition; the scheduler keeps no state","body":"Phase 1 of #1725: every scheduler tick asks every scheduled task, and the task's own declaration carries the whole answer. The engine keeps no scheduling state and no calendar of its own.

## Two fields, one sentence

`trigger` says **who mints an occurrence**; `preconditions` says **what must then hold**.

- `trigger: "schedule"` — asked by the scheduler at every tick.
- `trigger: "request"` — asked by nobody. It runs only from an item somebody creates (a mark, a hand-created item, a `--wake`, a chain link, a fan-out target), at whose pick its conditions are judged *exactly* as a scheduled task's are.

`isScheduledTask(decl)` is now a field read — no terms to load, no shape to interpret. `preconditions` stays optional and means only "requires nothing".

| term | holds when |
|---|---|
| `due:<daily\|weekly\|monthly>` | no run of the task started or ended since that cadence's most recent anchor on the repo's schedule |
| `last-run-over:<12h\|1d\|7d>` | the task's newest run started more than that long ago, or none in the 40-day horizon |
| `last-run-not-failed` | the task's newest run is not at a failure park — the opt-in that stops a task past its own failure |

Two earlier spellings of this were tried and are recorded in DESIGN §15.33 with the ground each lost on: a `woken` term (retired on review — "somebody created my item" is true of every run), and then the **shape** of `preconditions` (retired on review as cryptic: `["none"]` and no key at all were a keystroke apart and meant opposite things, and it made a scheduling question need the task's own terms loaded to answer, which is how one call site came to answer it wrong).

Two pairings the shape could not have caught, both now rejected by `task-declaration-shape`:

- A `schedule` task whose condition reads the item itself — the tick carries no item, so the term errors every hour instead of declining.
- A `request` task carrying a cadence term. **Writing S79 turned this up as a defect:** every occurrence of a request task is one somebody created, every such item carries `Woken:`, and a wake stands in for the cadence — so the term declines no run and only reads as though it limits the lever. My first draft of the scenario asserted the opposite and the simulator disagreed.

## An origin of its own

`task:origin:ad-hoc` carried two unlike things. `task:origin:manual` is now the second: an occurrence of a **declared task** somebody pulled the lever on, as against somebody's own issue adopted as the work item itself. Both stay exempt from the janitor's supersede rule, for reasons the comment now gives separately — an ad-hoc park because every ad-hoc item runs the same task over a different subject (#1498), a manual park because a pulled run is usually scoped by a qualifier the task's next clean occurrence did not cover. The dashboard's flows lane, which exists to show what people asked for, shows both.

## Retired, and how members converge

`frequency` and `none` are retired. The contract's door reads a legacy `frequency` as the cadence term plus the trigger it always meant (`manual` → `trigger: "request"` and no term), and derives `trigger` for a declaration stating none from exactly what the predicate read before — verified against all 28 canon declarations before they were given the field, so nothing changed behaviour. `legacy-task-fields` reports both; the `task-cadence-terms` record writes both into members' own local `task.json` files as anchored text on their nightly update, gated on the member's mount reading *both* (an older calendar rejects `due:daily`; an older schema is `additionalProperties: false` and would call a stated trigger an illegal key). #1732 retires the field door, #1789 the trigger derivation.

## The mechanism

- A `runs` signal — the task's own unqualified work items an executor picked, newest first, the item under evaluation excluded — is what the three terms read, and it sets every other signal's window. **A run begins at the pick**: an item still wearing `blocked` or `waiting-for-executor`, open or closed, is not a run (the simulator found F32).
- The run-history terms are judged first, over the queue the run already fetched, so a task whose cadence declines collects nothing else. A yes files a ready planned item, a no is one log line, an ask the scheduler cannot decide fails open.
- One live item per task is the engine's only invariant. A parked item is not live: the next occurrence is filed beside it unless the task declares `last-run-not-failed`. The schedule board, the first-window booking and the engine-owned lane hold are deleted.
- Rebasing brought in rule I (#1785), whose standing test was passing a frequency string into a predicate that now takes a boolean — so it silently stopped firing. Re-typed, and its posted comment no longer promises to release a lane that a park no longer holds.

## What changed where

- `packs/claudinite-tasks/` — `task-contract.mjs` (the two doors, `TRIGGERS`, `isScheduledTask`), `task.schema.json`, `calendar.mjs`, `precondition-policy.mjs`, `discover.mjs` (terms loaded before the door, so it can see them), the two checks, `signals/`, `queue/` (stateless run, `Woken:`, `itemFacts`, `ORIGIN_MANUAL`, janitor), the migration record; tests for all of it.
- `engine/migrations/` — the anchored-text rewrite, now both fields, and its registry op.
- Every pack's `tasks/*/task.json`, and the per-pack tests and READMEs.
- `packs/claudinite-dashboard/` — the roster reads the trigger, with the page's own copy of the door pinned to the contract's over one vector set.
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/test/sim/` and `docs/tasks-dispatch/SCENARIOS.md` — the simulator models the field as the engine writes it (neutering its door turns 59 scenarios red); S74–S79.
- `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` §5 and §15.33, `docs/task-preconditions/DESIGN.md`, the `writing-tasks` skill.

Closes #1731

## Growth-extract triage: PRs #1612–#1800

**Method:** Fetched full PR bodies for ~20 of the highest-friction-looking PRs (by title) plus `get_reviews`/`get_comments` for several. Finding: this repo's PRs carry **no GitHub-native review threads** — every `get_reviews`/`get_comments` call returned `[]`. All review happens in conversation before the squash-merge, and any friction narrative is self-reported by the author inside the PR body. So the analysis below is drawn entirely from PR-body admissions, not comment threads.

### Candidates worth flagging

**1. PR #1733 — a config shape that meant opposite things a keystroke apart caused a real call-site bug.**
Quote: *"the shape of `preconditions` (retired on review as cryptic: `[\"none\"]` and no key at all were a keystroke apart and meant opposite things, and it made a scheduling question need the task's own terms loaded to answer, which is how one call site came to answer it wrong)."*
This is a genuine, generalizable API/schema lesson — not the substance of the PR's landed design (which is the *replacement* shape), and not yet stated anywhere in RULES.md as far as I found. The closest existing rules are about unknown-vs-zero encoding and legacy-spelling normalization, neither of which covers "two near-identical spellings meaning opposite things is itself a hazard worth naming when designing any declaration shape." **Assessment: novel, worth a short rule** (e.g., under "Deciding where a config value or a classification lives" territory in the local pack) — something like: a value's presence/absence or an empty-vs-populated collection should never be the sole signal distinguishing two opposite meanings; make the opposite states name themselves.

**2. PR #1733 — a rebase silently broke a previously-firing rule via a type change, caught only by chance.**
Quote: *"Rebasing brought in rule I (#1785), whose standing test was passing a frequency string into a predicate that now takes a boolean — so it silently stopped firing."*
This is a real near-miss: changing what type a widely-called predicate accepts (string cadence → boolean) let an existing caller keep "passing" its test while the guard it exercised quietly went inert — not an error, a silent no-op. It was caught only because two large PRs happened to rebase against each other in the same day, not by CI. This is adjacent to but distinct from existing rules on renames/classification defaults — none of those specifically warn about a **predicate's accepted-type change causing a stale caller to silently stop firing** rather than throw. **Assessment: novel and fairly high-value** — worth a rule like "when narrowing or changing the type a shared predicate accepts, grep every caller and prefer a signature change that makes a stale caller throw, never one that lets it silently pass with no effect."

### Investigated and judged already-covered (not reporting as new signal)

- **#1773 → #1787**: a hand-fix for one known "blocking action check missing `since`" instance missed sibling instances in the same source PR, requiring a follow-up PR to build the actual check. This is a real instance of *not* following the already-stated ladder rule ("author the assurance first... and only then make the fixes"), but the rule itself already exists — this is a compliance gap, not a missing lesson.
- **#1671**'s flagged "design call for you to keep or revert" (making Stop-time guard re-judging always-advisory): I verified against `engine/checks/README.md` that this landed and is complementary to, not in conflict with, #1773/#1787's `since`-dating fix (they solve different problems: retroactive Stop-time conviction vs. live PreToolUse blocking of mid-flight sessions). Not a real unresolved tension.
- **#1786** (10 days vs. author's proposed 3 weeks; wide vs. narrow scope): normal owner value-calls during design, fully captured in the landed rule text.
- **#1737** (migration converter left dangling imports, froze a fleet member for days): the systemic risk (a blocking failure park never self-heals) is exactly what #1786's janitor rule I now bounds; the specific converter fix is a single call site, excluded per your criteria.
- **#1793**'s check-widening to a "structurally identical sibling" is a correct *application* of an existing rule, not a violation or new lesson.
- **#1734**'s aside about the pretooluse skill gate missing subagent transcript visibility is harness/framework loading mechanics — explicitly out of scope per your instructions.

### Bottom line
Out of ~20 PRs read in full, only #1733 yields two genuinely novel process/design lessons (both above); everything else that looked like friction resolves to either already-landed rules, normal design iteration fully captured by the commit, or excluded categories. This is consistent with an actively-curated repo where most friction gets absorbed same-day.

## Findings — 33 conversation-log files scanned

Scanned all 33 captures (timestamp/tool-count triage over every file, then `is_error`-filtered tool_result extraction — not raw keyword grep, which false-positives heavily on pack-prose text being read/edited into the transcript, e.g. RULES.md containing the word "misunderstood" or engine source containing the literal string "skill-not-loaded"). Most files are clean single-pass unattended queue runs with 0–7 real errors and no actionable pattern. Two files clear the bar with measured, repeated friction:

### Candidate 1 — skill-gate thrashing across a multi-file test sweep
**File:** `2026-09-06T0636Z--issue-1727--94d2f6a1-181d-5d98-bd45-1ebe8d1ee1a3.jsonl` (issue 1727)

The agent swept many test files across several packs (`claudinite-dashboard`, `claudinite-tasks`, `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`, `basics`) to fix `test(` calls, calling `Edit`/`Write` on each **before** loading the skill that pack's PreToolUse hook requires (`writing-tests`, later also `writing-tasks`, `writing-claudinite-skills`). Every attempt on an ungated file was refused with `skill-not-loaded ... needs writing-tests`.

Measured: **70** `is_error` `skill-not-loaded` tool_results between L756 (`2026-09-05T18:12:20.626Z`) and L1080 (`2026-09-05T18:17:39.509Z`) — 72 to 319 seconds of pure blocked-retry churn. Sample:
```
L755 Edit board.test.mjs         → L756 skill-not-loaded needs writing-tests
L757 Edit board.test.mjs (retry) → L758 skill-not-loaded needs writing-tests
L759 Edit cache.test.mjs         → L760 skill-not-loaded needs writing-tests
...
```
The skill was eventually loaded at L790, but the pattern **recurred** three more times later in the same run (L803, L1026, L1294 all re-invoke `writing-tests`/`writing-tasks`/`writing-claudinite-skills`), each preceded by fresh blocked edits on newly-touched files/packs. No other file in the batch came close — the next-highest real `skill-not-loaded` count elsewhere is 13 (issue 1672/327a7a86) vs. 70 here.

**Candidate rule sketch:** before starting a sweep that touches many files across multiple packs, survey the full target file list once and load every skill its paths force (`writing-tests`, plus any pack-specific one) up front, rather than discovering each requirement file-by-file through the hook's denial. Likely lands as a `basics`/RULES.md "Harness-tool contracts" bullet (sibling to the existing "Calling Edit" / "Polling with an until loop" entries).

### Candidate 2 — retrying ever-cleverer Bash forms against the worktree-isolation guard
**File:** `2026-09-06T1108Z--issue-1672--327a7a86-dda9-5866-8ecc-a895bd527291.jsonl` (issue 1672, a 9-growth-promote-PR consolidation)

Running inside a worktree-isolated agent (`/.claude/worktrees/agent-a04522e7b0c86e239`), Bash refuses any command it can't statically prove stays off `git` outside the worktree. The agent hit this repeatedly with **different** workaround shapes, each also refused, instead of dropping to a plain literal form:
```
22:31:07  for b in <branches...>; do git ...      → "names git in a form too complex to verify"
22:31:14  (same loop, retried)                     → same refusal
22:36:30  python3 - <<'EOF' ... references git ... → "feeds python text naming git in a plain command"
22:37:34  python3 heredoc again                     → same refusal
22:57:12  node --test $(git ls-files ...)           → "names git in a form too complex to verify"
22:57:18  node --test $(cat testfiles.txt)          → "runs node with a value computed at runtime"
22:57:22  xargs -a testfiles.txt node --test        → "runs xargs with -a in a plain command"
23:00:31  for p in <packs>; do node check-rules.mjs  → "names git in a form too complex to verify"
23:00:49  p="git"; p+="-github"; node check-rules.mjs → same refusal
```
Measured: **9** distinct blocked commands (all confirmed `is_error`) spanning `22:31:07` → `23:00:50`, i.e. ~29 minutes of wall-clock with repeated one-shot detours, none reusing the lesson from the prior refusal.

**Candidate rule sketch:** in a worktree-isolated agent, once Bash refuses a command as "too complex to verify," don't iterate through other clever forms (loops over names, heredocs mentioning git as text, `$(...)`-computed arguments, `xargs -a`, string-built variables) — switch immediately to the plain, literal, non-substituted form, since the guard is a syntactic verifier, not an intent checker. Same "Harness-tool contracts" home as candidate 1.

### Not pursued
- Merge-conflict `Edit` mismatches (3 "String to replace not found" hits, same file/issue) — isolated single retries during genuine manual conflict resolution, not a repeated loop; below the bar.
- The many multi-hour timestamp gaps across files sharing session UUIDs (e.g. issue 1736's 93-hour span, issue 1672's 69-hour span) — these are session-resume boundaries (harness/session-scheduling mechanics), not agent-caused idle waiting; per the local rules this is "engine plumbing," not a project lesson.
- `misunderstood`/`error`/`failed` raw keyword hits in most files were false positives from RULES.md/engine source text being read or edited into the transcript, not real friction.

No human-clarification-round-trip signal appeared in any file — consistent with these being unattended queue-executor sessions as expected.

{"number":1733,"title":"Scheduling is the task's own precondition; the scheduler keeps no state","body":"Phase 1 of #1725: every scheduler tick asks every scheduled task, and the task's own declaration carries the whole answer. The engine keeps no scheduling state and no calendar of its own.

## Two fields, one sentence

`trigger` says **who mints an occurrence**; `preconditions` says **what must then hold**.

- `trigger: "schedule"` — asked by the scheduler at every tick.
- `trigger: "request"` — asked by nobody. It runs only from an item somebody creates (a mark, a hand-created item, a `--wake`, a chain link, a fan-out target), at whose pick its conditions are judged *exactly* as a scheduled task's are.

`isScheduledTask(decl)` is now a field read — no terms to load, no shape to interpret. `preconditions` stays optional and means only "requires nothing".

| term | holds when |
|---|---|
| `due:<daily\|weekly\|monthly>` | no run of the task started or ended since that cadence's most recent anchor on the repo's schedule |
| `last-run-over:<12h\|1d\|7d>` | the task's newest run started more than that long ago, or none in the 40-day horizon |
| `last-run-not-failed` | the task's newest run is not at a failure park — the opt-in that stops a task past its own failure |

Two earlier spellings of this were tried and are recorded in DESIGN §15.33 with the ground each lost on: a `woken` term (retired on review — "somebody created my item" is true of every run), and then the **shape** of `preconditions` (retired on review as cryptic: `["none"]` and no key at all were a keystroke apart and meant opposite things, and it made a scheduling question need the task's own terms loaded to answer, which is how one call site came to answer it wrong).

Two pairings the shape could not have caught, both now rejected by `task-declaration-shape`:

- A `schedule` task whose condition reads the item itself — the tick carries no item, so the term errors every hour instead of declining.
- A `request` task carrying a cadence term. **Writing S79 turned this up as a defect:** every occurrence of a request task is one somebody created, every such item carries `Woken:`, and a wake stands in for the cadence — so the term declines no run and only reads as though it limits the lever. My first draft of the scenario asserted the opposite and the simulator disagreed.

## An origin of its own

`task:origin:ad-hoc` carried two unlike things. `task:origin:manual` is now the second: an occurrence of a **declared task** somebody pulled the lever on, as against somebody's own issue adopted as the work item itself. Both stay exempt from the janitor's supersede rule, for reasons the comment now gives separately — an ad-hoc park because every ad-hoc item runs the same task over a different subject (#1498), a manual park because a pulled run is usually scoped by a qualifier the task's next clean occurrence did not cover. The dashboard's flows lane, which exists to show what people asked for, shows both.

## Retired, and how members converge

`frequency` and `none` are retired. The contract's door reads a legacy `frequency` as the cadence term plus the trigger it always meant (`manual` → `trigger: "request"` and no term), and derives `trigger` for a declaration stating none from exactly what the predicate read before — verified against all 28 canon declarations before they were given the field, so nothing changed behaviour. `legacy-task-fields` reports both; the `task-cadence-terms` record writes both into members' own local `task.json` files as anchored text on their nightly update, gated on the member's mount reading *both* (an older calendar rejects `due:daily`; an older schema is `additionalProperties: false` and would call a stated trigger an illegal key). #1732 retires the field door, #1789 the trigger derivation.

## The mechanism

- A `runs` signal — the task's own unqualified work items an executor picked, newest first, the item under evaluation excluded — is what the three terms read, and it sets every other signal's window. **A run begins at the pick**: an item still wearing `blocked` or `waiting-for-executor`, open or closed, is not a run (the simulator found F32).
- The run-history terms are judged first, over the queue the run already fetched, so a task whose cadence declines collects nothing else. A yes files a ready planned item, a no is one log line, an ask the scheduler cannot decide fails open.
- One live item per task is the engine's only invariant. A parked item is not live: the next occurrence is filed beside it unless the task declares `last-run-not-failed`. The schedule board, the first-window booking and the engine-owned lane hold are deleted.
- Rebasing brought in rule I (#1785), whose standing test was passing a frequency string into a predicate that now takes a boolean — so it silently stopped firing. Re-typed, and its posted comment no longer promises to release a lane that a park no longer holds.

## What changed where

- `packs/claudinite-tasks/` — `task-contract.mjs` (the two doors, `TRIGGERS`, `isScheduledTask`), `task.schema.json`, `calendar.mjs`, `precondition-policy.mjs`, `discover.mjs` (terms loaded before the door, so it can see them), the two checks, `signals/`, `queue/` (stateless run, `Woken:`, `itemFacts`, `ORIGIN_MANUAL`, janitor), the migration record; tests for all of it.
- `engine/migrations/` — the anchored-text rewrite, now both fields, and its registry op.
- Every pack's `tasks/*/task.json`, and the per-pack tests and READMEs.
- `packs/claudinite-dashboard/` — the roster reads the trigger, with the page's own copy of the door pinned to the contract's over one vector set.
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/test/sim/` and `docs/tasks-dispatch/SCENARIOS.md` — the simulator models the field as the engine writes it (neutering its door turns 59 scenarios red); S74–S79.
- `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` §5 and §15.33, `docs/task-preconditions/DESIGN.md`, the `writing-tasks` skill.

Closes #1731

---
name: running-the-suite
description: Running this repo's test suite — the one command that covers it, reading a run's output from a file instead of re-running it, iterating on the tests an edit touches, and staging a new test file before certifying a run. Use before any node --test.
metadata:
  force-load-on-tool-calls:
    - 'Bash.command /\bnode\s+--test\b/'
---

# Running the suite

- **The whole suite is one command** — `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. There is no test
  script, `node --test <dir>` does not recurse, and a bash glob without `globstar` reached 37 of 65
  files; `ci.yml`'s array is not authoritative.
- **Read a run's output from a file** — redirect one run and grep that file for the slice you need;
  never re-run the ~55s suite to re-slice unchanged output. (1)
- **`git add` a new test file before certifying a run green** — `git ls-files` excludes an unstaged
  file, so the run never executed it; the `untracked-test-file` finding at Stop says which. (2)
- **Iterating on a sweep across many files** — run only the test files the edit touches, plus

  whole-tree aggregates whose verdict cannot turn on one file. (3)

2	name: writing-pack-prose
3	description: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.

6	    - "**/packs/*/RULES.md"
7	    - "**/packs/*/skills/*/SKILL.md"

9	
10	# Writing pack prose
11	
12	Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
13	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.
14	
15	**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
16	[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
17	principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
18	the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
19	layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.
20	
21	## The ration
22	
23	Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
24	forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.
25	
26	- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
27	  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
28	  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
29	- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
30	  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
31	- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
32	  trigger.
33	- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
34	  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
35	  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
36	  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs in the references doc
37	  below.
38	- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
39	  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
40	  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
41	  a moment no file edit predicts stays prose, however activity-shaped it reads. (2)
42	
43	## Shape a rule so it fires
44	
45	- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
46	  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
47	  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
48	  reader to it.
49	- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
50	  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
51	  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
52	- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
53	  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
54	  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
55	- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
56	  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
57	- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
58	  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
59	  to three neighbouring bullets.
60	- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
61	  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
62	  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
63	- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
64	  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
65	- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
66	  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
67	  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
68	- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
69	  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
70	  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
71	  you report the change.
72	- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
73	  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
74	- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
75	  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
76	  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
77	  it.
78	- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
79	  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
80	  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
81	- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
82	  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
83	  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
84	  hand-built command. (1)
85	- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
86	  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
87	- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
88	  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
89	- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
90	  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
91	  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
92	  reader doesn't need at act time goes to the references doc below.
93	- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
94	  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
95	  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
96	  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
97	  teaches a world the reader won't find.
98	- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
99	  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.
100	
101	## The references doc — where a rule's rationale lives
102	
103	A pack keeps **one** `references.md` beside its `RULES.md`, servicing all of the pack's prose
104	files and its checks. It exists for maintenance and review — the periodic pass that asks
105	whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written — never for daily agentic
106	work: no rule sends its reader there, and no session loads it. So it stays in the repo that
107	owns the pack and never vendors: a member mounting a canon pack receives the rules, not the
108	reasoning behind them, and the pass that reaffirms them runs where the pack lives.
109	
110	- **Adding a rule that has a rationale** — write the brief rule in `RULES.md` (or the skill),
111	  and put the reason in `references.md`. End the rule with the bare marker — `… never a
112	  filesystem walk. (3)` — and nothing else: don't name the references file, don't link it,
113	  don't ask the reader to follow anything. Not every rule needs one; a rule whose reason is
114	  self-evident from its consequence clause carries no marker.
115	- **Writing the entry** — one bullet per entry, keyed by the citing file's own namespace:
116	  `- **(RULES-3)** <reason>` for a rule in `RULES.md`, `- **(<skill-name>-3)** <reason>` for a
117	  line in that skill's `SKILL.md`; the marker in the prose file stays the bare `(3)` and
118	  resolves within its own file's namespace. Write the reason so a future review can **reaffirm
119	  the rule from it**: what would have to be true for the rule to be retired.
120	  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
121	    the error, the measured cost).
122	  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
123	  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it.
124	- **Numbering** — numbers are stable identifiers, not positions: the next entry takes its
125	  file's next unused number, a removed entry leaves a gap, and nothing ever renumbers (a
126	  renumber breaks every marker at once). One entry may serve several rules in its file; a rule
127	  may cite several entries (`(3, 7)`).
128	- **A check's rationale** — the entry points at the check, since a declaration admits no
129	  comment and no new key: `- **(check:growth-write-scope)** <reason>`, same reaffirmation
130	  standard. There is no marker on the check side.
131	- **Removing a rule or check** — remove its entry in the same change, unless another rule
132	  still cites it.
133	
134	The `references-integrity` check holds the mechanism together: every marker must resolve to an
135	entry in the pack's own `references.md`, and every `check:` entry must name a check the pack
136	still carries. The `rule-revalidation` task is the mechanism's consumer — it reaffirms
137	referenced rules and checks against their recorded reasons on its weekly pass.
138	
139	## Migrating an existing pack onto the references doc
140	
141	An existing pack — a repo's local pack, or a shared canon pack worked on canon-side (a member
142	never edits the mounted canon) — migrates opportunistically, one pack per pass, whenever a pass
143	is already editing it. An unmarked rule stays valid forever, so there is no fleet sweep to
144	force and no straggler to chase; the check only judges markers that exist.
145	
146	1. **Create `references.md`** beside the pack's `RULES.md` on its first entry, not before.
147	2. **Work each rule**: keep the act-time consequence clause inline; move review-only rationale —
148	   the evidence story, inline issue ids, a cost the reader doesn't need mid-act — into an entry
149	   and end the rule with its marker. Shrink-only on the rules side: a rule may lose review-only
150	   rationale in this pass, never gain text.
151	3. **Recover the missing reasons from history, source-first**: for a rule that states no reason,
152	   read the commit that added it and that commit's PR and issue *before* re-reading the rule —
153	   derive the entry from the source, then diff against what the rule implied. The commit
154	   message, PR body and issue discussion are where this corpus already keeps a rule's evidence.
155	4. **Never invent an entry.** A rule whose reason can't be recovered stays unmarked — an audit
156	   or the `rule-revalidation` pass judges whether it still earns its place; a plausible-sounding
157	   fabricated rationale would let a future review reaffirm a rule on false grounds.
158	5. **Cover the checks** worth reaffirming with `check:` entries the same way, from their `why`
159	   text and their adding commit's PR.
160	
161	## Evidence
162	
163	The commit and its PR remain the archive — dates, session ids, quoted exchanges and the story
164	of the incident live there, never in the rule. What the references doc takes from them is only
165	the **reaffirmable core**: the reason and the minimum evidence a future review needs to re-test
166	it. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument — a cost the
167	reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.
168

- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
  a moment no file edit predicts stays prose, however activity-shaped it reads. (2)

## Shape a rule so it fires

- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
  reader to it.
- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
  to three neighbouring bullets.
- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
  you report the change.
- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
  it.
- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
  hand-built command. (1)
- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
  reader doesn't need at act time goes to the references doc below.
- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
  teaches a world the reader won't find.
- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.

## The references doc — where a rule's rationale lives

A pack keeps **one** `references.md` beside its `RULES.md`, servicing all of the pack's prose
files and its checks. It exists for maintenance and review — the periodic pass that asks
whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written — never for daily agentic
work: no rule sends its reader there, and no session loads it. So it stays in the repo that
owns the pack and never vendors: a member mounting a canon pack receives the rules, not the
reasoning behind them, and the pass that reaffirms them runs where the pack lives.

- **Adding a rule that has a rationale** — write the brief rule in `RULES.md` (or the skill),
  and put the reason in `references.md`. End the rule with the bare marker — `… never a
  filesystem walk. (3)` — and nothing else: don't name the references file, don't link it,
  don't ask the reader to follow anything. Not every rule needs one; a rule whose reason is
  self-evident from its consequence clause carries no marker.
- **Writing the entry** — one bullet per entry, keyed by the citing file's own namespace:
  `- **(RULES-3)** <reason>` for a rule in `RULES.md`, `- **(<skill-name>-3)** <reason>` for a
  line in that skill's `SKILL.md`; the marker in the prose file stays the bare `(3)` and
  resolves within its own file's namespace. Write the reason so a future review can **reaffirm
  the rule from it**: what would have to be true for the rule to be retired.
  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
    the error, the measured cost).
  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it.
- **Numbering** — numbers are stable identifiers, not positions: the next entry takes its
  file's next unused number, a removed entry leaves a gap, and nothing ever renumbers (a
  renumber breaks every marker at once). One entry may serve several rules in its file; a rule
  may cite several entries (`(3, 7)`).
- **A check's rationale** — the entry points at the check, since a declaration admits no
  comment and no new key: `- **(check:growth-write-scope)** <reason>`, same reaffirmation
  standard. There is no marker on the check side.
- **Removing a rule or check** — remove its entry in the same change, unless another rule
  still cites it.

The `references-integrity` check holds the mechanism together: every marker must resolve to an
entry in the pack's own `references.md`, and every `check:` entry must name a check the pack
still carries. The `rule-revalidation` task is the mechanism's consumer — it reaffirms
referenced rules and checks against their recorded reasons on its weekly pass.

## Migrating an existing pack onto the references doc

An existing pack — a repo's local pack, or a shared canon pack worked on canon-side (a member
never edits the mounted canon) — migrates opportunistically, one pack per pass, whenever a pass
is already editing it. An unmarked rule stays valid forever, so there is no fleet sweep to
force and no straggler to chase; the check only judges markers that exist.

1. **Create `references.md`** beside the pack's `RULES.md` on its first entry, not before.
2. **Work each rule**: keep the act-time consequence clause inline; move review-only rationale —
   the evidence story, inline issue ids, a cost the reader doesn't need mid-act — into an entry
   and end the rule with its marker. Shrink-only on the rules side: a rule may lose review-only
   rationale in this pass, never gain text.
3. **Recover the missing reasons from history, source-first**: for a rule that states no reason,
   read the commit that added it and that commit's PR and issue *before* re-reading the rule —
   derive the entry from the source, then diff against what the rule implied. The commit
   message, PR body and issue discussion are where this corpus already keeps a rule's evidence.
4. **Never invent an entry.** A rule whose reason can't be recovered stays unmarked — an audit
   or the `rule-revalidation` pass judges whether it still earns its place; a plausible-sounding
   fabricated rationale would let a future review reaffirm a rule on false grounds.
5. **Cover the checks** worth reaffirming with `check:` entries the same way, from their `why`
   text and their adding commit's PR.

## Evidence

The commit and its PR remain the archive — dates, session ids, quoted exchanges and the story
of the incident live there, never in the rule. What the references doc takes from them is only
the **reaffirmable core**: the reason and the minimum evidence a future review needs to re-test
it. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument — a cost the
reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.

386	
387	- **Building a simulator for a stateful engine mechanism** — model what the engine's code actually
388	  *writes*, never the rule's stated *intent*. A sim advancing state wherever the rule's description
389	  matches is correct by construction and blind to where the two diverge.
390	
391	- **Asserting a mid-run invariant** — capture it at the exact moment the state holds. By the end
392	  of the run, normal convergence has cleared the evidence.
393	
394	- **Writing a regression test that pins a policy or convention decision** — assert the
395	  behavior/invariant the decision requires, never a literal sentence quoted from a doc: a
396	  sentence-matching test stays green even while a sibling doc states the opposite, certifying the
397	  contradiction instead of catching it.
398	
399	- **A test that derives its answer by walking git history** — guard explicitly against a shallow
400	  clone and fail loudly. It otherwise passes vacuously exactly when the real answer needs history
401	  it doesn't have. (56)
402	
403	
404	- **Restoring source after a deliberate see-it-fail mutation** — `git checkout -- <file>` at the
405	  moment of mutating, never a `.bak` taken earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in
406	  between. (57)
407	
408	
409	- **Surveying whether something exists in the tree** — a code-search hit is evidence; a miss is
410	  not. Survey by reading each file.
411	
412	- **Documenting or relying on a named knob** — grep for the code that reads it and the code that
413	  writes it first. The corpus naming it is not evidence it exists; all three misses are real
414	  here. (62)
415	
416	- **Deleting a writer** — it is the same change as marking its series historical. Its rows keep
417	  counting plausibly until the retention window ages out, then count nothing. (63)
418	
419	- **Renaming an entity** — sweep for references in code and comments, don't change historical
420	  records, and re-render generated files rather than editing them by hand.
421	
422	- **Sweeping a rename mid-migration across many PRs** — a file added or rewritten after the sweep
423	  starts can independently reinvent the retired constant as a comparison key; a state comparison
424	  against it fails silently, with no error and no failing test, only a wrong count. (3)
425	
426	- **Renaming a word that is also stored data** (a counter key, a wire word, a label) — rename it
427	  on the **decode** side too, or the next encode writes those historical counts as `null`,
428	  silently and only for the old rows.
429	
430	- **A second rename of one name** — map every legacy spelling straight to today's, never chaining
431	  one normalization onto the last, so the oldest vocabulary still normalizes in a single pass. (64)
432	
433	- **Writing a "this period is covered" marker in an idempotent pipeline** — write it strictly
434	  after the durable effect it guards, and scope it to the *declined* case only. A go verdict's
435	  coverage is judged by the item it created, never by the row.
436	
437	- **Verifying a bulk file-move or rewrite sweep preserved content** — check a structural invariant
438	  count before and after (total `test(` calls across the touched files). One sweep truncated 46
439	  test files to zero bytes and every one still "passed".
440	
441	## Editing, branching and merging here
442	
443	
444	
445	- **A JSON target nested inside an array within an entry object** — parse and rewrite
446	  structurally, preserving key order and `via`/`config`/answers by hand. An anchored regex cannot
447	  cross the nested closing bracket, and a fixture without that nesting proves nothing. (65)
448	
449	- **Returning to a branch that waited** — after `git fetch`, re-verify the *premise* unasked: say
450	  whether the problem is still there and what survives. This repo auto-merges its own PRs on top of
451	  migrations that retire whole directories.
452	
453	
454	- **Merging a PR that has sat open across many `main` commits** — check its current
455	  `mergeable_state`, not an old green CI run. A structural change on `main` since (a directory
456	  move, a renamed path) can turn a once-clean branch conflicted without a new run ever failing.
457	
458	- **After a PR lands by squash-merge** — `git remote prune origin` before touching that branch
459	  again. GitHub deletes the head ref here, so a stale tracking ref makes the next push reject and
460	  the stop hook report phantom local work. (67)
461	
462	
463	
464	- **Merging in a session that also has a consumer repo in its sources** — resolve the merge skill
465	  by *target repo*, not by which matched first. The consumer's wins on name, silently skipping the
466	  canon-only post-merge conversation capture
467	  (`node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), which is part of the merge.
468	
469	- **Having work that completes or corrects an open PR** — put it on that PR's branch. A dispatch
470	  prompt's designated branch routes work, not review; splitting gives the owner two gates for one
471	  decision.
472	
473	- **Wanting to combine two PRs** — update the one you're keeping and close the other. Never push
474	  one's branch onto the other's base: GitHub marks a PR merged once its head is reachable, and a
475	  later `state: closed` is a no-op. Check the API's `merged` field before reporting.
476	
477	- **Being asked "should no X decide this?"** — it questions whether the decision exists at all;
478	  never answer by relocating the knob one rung out. Ask who would set it differently and why that
479	  can't be read off the structure.
480	
481	- **Facing a retry across a call whose outcome you cannot observe** — check whether declining to
482	  retry removes the uncertainty before building dedup machinery to manage it.
483	
484	- **Writing a regex import-path rewriter for a bulk file-move** — anchor to real import/export
485	  syntax (line-start, or after a specific separator), never a bare `from '...'` searched across the
486	  whole text. A fixture embedding import syntax as string data matches identically and is corrupted.
487	
488	- **Running the prose-to-checks sweep here** — the worklist is
489	  `docs/declarative-checks/rule-inventory.md`, every rule classified by the moment that could
490	  carry it; convert from its A–F rows, and correct a mis-read row there, dated, rather than
491	  re-deriving the class.
